title: Merge sort
summary: Split in half, sort each half, merge: O(n log n) by divide and conquer.

steps.title: Merging two sorted arrays
body: Two arrays that are **already sorted** can be combined in one pass. Keep a finger on the front of each (`i` and `j`); copy whichever value is smaller into the result and move that finger on. When one side runs out, copy the rest of the other.
Each step places one item, so merging `n` items is `O(n)`. Watch `i`, `j` and `k` advance.

steps.prompt: This merge counts its comparisons. What does it print?
steps.explain: Every left value is smaller than 4, so three comparisons empty the left side. The right side is then copied with no comparisons at all.

steps.title: Divide and conquer
body: **Merge sort** uses merging to sort anything:
1. An array of 0 or 1 items is already sorted.
2. Otherwise split it in half and **merge sort each half** (recursion).
Halving gives `log n` levels of splitting, and each level merges `n` items in total: **O(n log n)** time, always, whatever the input. The cost is `O(n)` extra memory for the merged arrays.
Watch the calls nest: `Sort` keeps splitting until the pieces are single items, then the merges rebuild them in order.

code: while (i < l.Length && j < r.Length) result[k++] = l[i] <= r[j] ? l[i++] : r[j++];

steps.prompt: Arrange the body of the recursive `MergeSort`.
steps.explain: The base case must come first, or the recursion never stops. The two halves can be sorted in either order.

steps.prompt: Merge sort on 1,024 items: how many levels of splitting are there before every piece is a single item?
steps.explain: 1,024 is 2¹⁰, so ten halvings. Each level merges all 1,024 items once: about 10 × 1,024 steps instead of a million.

steps.prompt: Complete the main merge loop. Taking from the left on a tie keeps equal items in their original order.
steps.explain: `i++` reads `l[i]` and then moves on. `++i` would skip an item.

steps.title: Merge
prompt: Write `int[] Merge(int[] l, int[] r)`: both inputs are sorted ascending; return a new sorted array with every item from both.
Use the two-finger technique, `O(n)`. No `Concat`, `OrderBy` or `Sort`.
solution: while (i < l.Length && j < r.Length) result[k++] = l[i] <= r[j] ? l[i++] : r[j++];
template: Dojo.Eq("left empty", new[] { 1, 2 }, Merge(new int[0], new[] { 1, 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("right empty", new[] { 5 }, Merge(new[] { 5 }, new int[0]));
Dojo.Eq("duplicates across sides", new[] { 1, 1, 2, 2 }, Merge(new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 1, 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("one side all smaller", new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }, Merge(new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 3, 4, 5 }));
hints: Three loops: while both have items, take the smaller; then copy what is left of `l`; then of `r`.

steps.title: Merge sort
prompt: Write `int[] MergeSort(int[] a)` that returns a **new** sorted array. Write your own `Merge` as well (copy it from the last step).
The tests sort 300,000 numbers. An `O(n²)` sort would need about 45 billion steps; merge sort needs about 6 million.
Slices like `a[..mid]` and `a[mid..]` copy part of an array.
solution: while (i < l.Length && j < r.Length) result[k++] = l[i] <= r[j] ? l[i++] : r[j++];
template: Dojo.Eq("an empty array", new int[0], MergeSort(new int[0]));

forbid.message: Does not call a library sort

hints: Recursive case: `return Merge(MergeSort(a[..mid]), MergeSort(a[mid..]));` with `mid = a.Length / 2`.
